planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in fall on a lean, rocky or serpentine-derived slope with sharp drainage; never amend the planting hole with compost or fertilizer, which encourages root rot in cultivated manzanitas.

directions: This finely textured, low-growing manzanita is restricted in the wild to the serpentine and metamorphic outcrops of the Klamath-Siskiyou region, where mineral-poor soil keeps competing shrubs at bay. In the garden it rewards the same lean, ultramafic-mimicking treatment: a gritty, unimproved slope, full sun, and strict drought once roots are established. Because only a small handful of specialty native-plant nurseries carry it, start from a young container plant rather than seed, and avoid heavy mulch or irrigation lines designed for ordinary perennial beds. It combines well with other serpentine specialists in a rock-garden or demonstration bed themed around unusual soil chemistry.
sources: California Native Plant Society Rare Plant Program

planting.note: Divide rhizome clumps in fall for fastest establishment, or sow fresh seed outdoors in fall for a full winter of cold, moist stratification ahead of spring germination.

directions: Howell's violet carpets the floor of Douglas-fir and oak-mixed woodlands with pale lavender-blue flowers in early spring, filling the gap before larger perennials leaf out. Give it humus-rich, consistently moist soil under open canopy, since it resents baking summer sun or dry compacted ground. It self-sows gently once settled, so site it where a drifting carpet under shrubs or along a shaded path edge is welcome rather than in a tightly bordered bed. A fall top-dressing of leaf litter mimics its native duff layer and keeps the shallow rhizomes from drying out.

planting.note: Divide established rhizome clumps in early fall, or sow fresh seed outdoors and cold-stratify over winter; expect slow, uneven germination the following spring.

directions: Shelton's violet stands apart from round-leaved woodland violets with deeply dissected, fan-shaped foliage and small yellow flowers veined in maroon, a plant of mixed-evergreen and dry pine woodland floors that dry out by midsummer. Plant it in duff-rich but fast-draining soil on a dappled slope and avoid heavy clay or constant irrigation, both of which rot the rhizomes. It goes gracefully summer-dormant once the canopy closes in, so pair it with later-emerging woodland companions to carry interest through the dry season.

planting.note: Sow outdoors in fall so seed receives 60-90 days of natural cold-moist stratification; established crowns can also be divided during winter dormancy.

directions: Among the tallest true shade perennials in cultivation, giant larkspur sends up marine-blue flower spikes above glossy, trollius-like foliage in a cool, high-canopy woodland setting. Keep it evenly moist through its spring growth and bloom, then allow somewhat drier conditions as it goes summer dormant. Site it away from grazing animals or curious children, since every part of the plant contains toxic alkaloids typical of the genus. It performs best under deciduous trees that leaf out after its spring growth spurt, giving it cool, bright light early and deeper shade later.

planting.note: Tuck rooted divisions into rocky, well-drained shaded crevices in fall ahead of winter rains; spore-grown nursery plugs establish well set out at the same time of year.

directions: Unusual among ferns for genuine drought tolerance, goldback fern flashes a powdery gold underside to its fronds when disturbed and thrives in rocky, shaded pockets that bake dry by midsummer. Resist the temptation to water it through the dry season, since constant moisture causes the rhizomes to rot — this species actually wants a dry summer dormancy to match its native dry shade under oak or madrone canopy. Once established in a crevice or bank with sharp drainage, it needs little attention for years and slowly spreads to fill the available rock pocket.

planting.note: Divide or layer rooted sections of the creeping mat in spring and press into constantly moist, shaded soil; sections spread and knit together within one growing season.

directions: Pacific golden saxifrage fills the wettest, darkest micro-sites in a shade garden — a streamside seep or the perpetually damp ground beneath a downspout — with a dense, low mat studded with tiny chartreuse spring flowers. It will not tolerate drying out even briefly, so reserve it for boggy spots rather than general shade borders. Once settled it forms an effective living mulch that suppresses weeds in conditions too wet and dark for most other groundcovers, and spreads readily from small divisions pressed into the mud.

planting.note: Nick or sand the hard seed coat and sow outdoors in fall for natural cold-moist stratification over winter; direct-sow where it will scramble through low shrubs rather than transplanting.

directions: This well-mannered native pea scrambles through low shrubs at a woodland margin, lifting blue-purple flowers on wiry stems without the smothering spread of introduced vetches. Give it lean, fast-draining soil and let it climb through sturdy companions rather than staking it formally, since rich or regularly watered beds produce floppy, weak growth. It is purely ornamental — the seeds share the toxic compound found in other Lathyrus species — so grow it for its flowers and light woodland-edge texture, not as a food crop.

planting.note: Set out nursery-grown container plugs in fall or early spring directly into rock crevices; this species transplants poorly bare-root or when divided from wild-collected clumps, so always start from actively growing container stock.

directions: A true rock-garden specialist rather than a woodland-floor fern, lace fern forms a tiny cushion of lacy gray-green fronds wedged into crevices of a dry stone wall or outcrop with partial overhead shade. Water sparingly once established, since it is adapted to long dry spells and will rot in rich, moisture-retentive soil. Buy it as an actively growing container plant rather than attempting to divide or relocate an existing clump, since it resents root disturbance and establishes slowly.

planting.note: Install container-grown plants in fall on a well-drained, lean slope at the bright edge of a woodland planting; semi-hardwood cuttings taken in late summer with rooting hormone are the standard nursery propagation route since seed is slow and erratic.

directions: A defining structural companion of the Pacific madrone woodland community, hairy manzanita carries cinnamon bark and clusters of white-to-pink spring flowers above evergreen foliage. Reserve it for the drier, brighter fringe of a woodland planting rather than deep shade, since flowering and fruit set both drop off noticeably in heavier shade. Give it acidic, lean soil mimicking its native rocky slopes and little to no summer water once established, as amended garden loam and regular irrigation both shorten its life considerably.
